title: The EC2 budget emergency brake cannot be tag-scoped — AWS budget actions take explicit InstanceIds
question: AC-085 and deploy/aws/00-account.sh both describe the spend emergency brake as a budget action stopping 'Project=ACMP instances'. AWS offers no such shape: `aws budgets create-budget-action --generate-cli-skeleton` shows SsmActionDefinition as {ActionSubType, Region, InstanceIds} — a list of instance IDs, no tag filter anywhere in the API. Two consequences: the action cannot exist before P25 launches instances, so nothing about it is verifiable today; and once created it is pinned to specific IDs and must be RE-POINTED whenever an instance is replaced, which for the routinely stopped/started on-demand UAT box is recurring maintenance rather than a one-off. The IAM half is unaffected and is now created automatically by 00-account.sh (verified live: action 1ed50a50, 100% ACTUAL, AUTOMATIC, STANDBY). Options for the EC2 half: (a) create it in P25 with the launched instance IDs and add re-pointing to the instance-replacement runbook; (b) replace it with an EventBridge rule on the budget SNS topic invoking a Lambda that stops instances BY TAG — the behaviour AC-085 actually describes; (c) accept the IAM deny action as the sole brake and record the reduced protection. AC-085 needs amending either way: it is unsatisfiable as written, and it says 120% while the script targets 100% FORECAST.
resolution: Option (a) PLUS automation — keep the native SSM STOP_EC2_INSTANCES action, but make P25's instance-launch script OWN the InstanceIds via create-or-update immediately after launch, the same idempotent pattern 06-github-oidc.sh already uses for the OIDC role. Re-verified from the live API this session: the skeleton confirms SsmActionDefinition is {ActionSubType, Region, InstanceIds} with no tag filter, so the premise stands. Option (b)'s EventBridge/Lambda was rejected as disproportionate — a function, an execution role, an SNS subscription and code to maintain, for a fleet of exactly two instances only ever created by a sanctioned script; it remains the right answer if instances ever start being created outside that path, the one case (a) does not cover. Option (c) was rejected outright because the IAM deny action does NOT reduce EXISTING spend: a deny policy blocks new API calls but a running t3.medium keeps billing, so (c) would leave the brake with no lever that actually lowers the bill. The decisive argument for automating the re-point rather than documenting it is the failure mode — a stale InstanceId does not error, it silently protects nothing, the same silent-failure shape as DEF-017 and DEF-018. TWO FINDINGS surfaced while resolving this. (i) The IAM deny action attaches to the IAM USER acmp-admin, and the account ROOT user cannot be restricted by IAM policies at all (only an Organizations SCP could; this is a standalone account). The operator is still doing CLI work as root, so while that holds the brake reads armed and constrains nobody — raising the P20 'switch off root' item from hygiene to guardrail-critical. (ii) A second pre-existing budget 'My Monthly Cost Budget' at $10 exists in the account, is not ours, and will alert well before acmp-monthly's $60; do not read its alerts as the ACMP brake firing.

title: trace_query cannot reach the decision layer — but the DEC->ADR link EXISTS as promoted_to; the gap is derivation, not missing data
question: Raised by the 2026-08-05 integrity audit, which found that not one of the 1042 trace edges touches a DEC- id and concluded the decision->architecture relationships 'exist only in prose'. The question asked whether to wire roughly forty DEC->ADR / DEC->scope-change edges, or to accept the decision layer as narrative-only.
resolution: RESOLVED 2026-08-06 as: NO ACTION on the package; record the convention; raise the derivation gap upstream. The premise was wrong twice over, and both corrections are the answer. FIRST, the DEC->ADR link is not prose — 18 of 30 decisions already carry it as a typed promoted_to field (DEC-001->ADR-0001, DEC-003->ADR-0003, DEC-005->ADR-0005, DEC-006->ADR-0004, DEC-007->ADR-0010, DEC-010->ADR-0005, DEC-012->ADR-0007, DEC-016->ADR-0007, DEC-018->ADR-0009, DEC-019->ADR-0006, DEC-020->ADR-0003, DEC-021->ADR-0002, DEC-022->ADR-0012, DEC-023->ADR-0001, DEC-024->ADR-0011, DEC-025->ADR-0008, DEC-027->ADR-0018, DEC-028->ADR-0006). SECOND, the 12 nulls are CORRECT, not omissions: promoted_to is populated exactly when a decision was promoted INTO an ADR, and null when the decision landed as a different kind of artifact. Reading the titles makes the convention self-evident — DEC-009 (exactly one committee, no multi-committee) and DEC-017 (scale ceiling <=20 users) are hard CONSTRAINTS, DEC-014 (availability 99.9%) is an NFR, DEC-029 (model P16-P19 as phase PH-4) is a planning decision that produced phases and slices, and DEC-031 is a reading rule producing no artifact. A decision that never became an ADR should have a null promoted_to; populating it would be fabrication. WHAT REMAINS TRUE is narrow: trace_query cannot reach the decision layer because promoted_to is never materialised into trace_edges, the table trace_query reads. That is a DERIVATION gap in the tamheed export rather than absent knowledge — the authorization chain is fully queryable today via entity_query on the decision rows. Raised as an upstream note for the tamheed plugin (derive trace_edges from promoted_to at export time), NOT as a blocker here. ONE CLAUSE OF THIS RESOLUTION WAS FACTUALLY WRONG AND IS CORRECTED 2026-08-08. It stated that 'tamheed 2.6.0 exposes no write path to trace_edges in any case (entity_upsert rejects both trace-edge and trace_edge)'. That is FALSE and was tested rather than re-reasoned: entity_upsert(type='trace-edge', ...) returns ok/applied:1 against the live package, and 'trace-edge' is a registered entity type in the plugin source (tamheed_server.py:77, commented 'write surface for relations') with its own INSERT OR IGNORE path (tamheed_server.py:263-265) and is documented as a write surface in the plugin's own server/README.md and SKILL.md. Only the underscore spelling 'trace_edge' is genuinely unknown. THE MISREADING HAS A ROOT CAUSE IN THE TOOL, not merely in the reader: entity_query(type='trace-edge') answers with the literal message "unknown entity type 'trace-edge'" (tamheed_server.py:306) for a type that is known and writable — the read surface reports the type as nonexistent rather than as non-queryable, and that false message is what this resolution believed. Reported upstream as findings_10 §A2. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE is the decision: wiring duplicate DEC->ADR edges was undesirable regardless of whether it was possible, because it would create two records of one fact that can drift apart — the same two-sources-of-truth anti-pattern seed-users.sh avoids by refusing to mirror Keycloak identity into the application database. The correct fix remains derivation at export time, upstream. ONE MODELLING EDGE ACCEPTED, not deferred: promoted_to models a 1:1 PROMOTION, but DEC-030 was not promoted — it AUTHORIZED four separate artifacts (SC-002 plus ADRs 0034-0037). 'Authorizes' is a distinct relation from 'promoted into'; the schema has neither a typed edge nor a multi-valued field for it. The affected population is essentially one decision, its text names all four targets explicitly and searchably, and stuffing one of the four ADRs into promoted_to would lose information while merely looking tidier. Left as prose, deliberately. STANDING GUIDANCE for future readers: do not read trace silence on a DEC- row as absent authorization — query the decision row's promoted_to and its text instead.

title: AC-076 names a method that is provably impossible — it can only ever be satisfied by ignoring its own instructions
question: AC-076 reads 'When the existing Playwright suite runs against E2E_WEB_URL=https://uat.acmp.anas7ammo.dev with E2E_KEYCLOAK_URL=https://uat.acmp.anas7ammo.dev/kc'. That second URL cannot work, and this is measured rather than argued (DEF-027): the suite's global-setup seeds its fixtures through the Keycloak ADMIN REST API after taking a master-realm token, and deploy/nginx/cloud-443.conf.template returns 404 for BOTH /kc/admin and /kc/realms/master BY DESIGN, because everything under /kc/ becomes publicly reachable the moment 443 exists. AC-081 is partly Met on exactly that deny, so the deny is not negotiable. The AC is therefore in the state AC-085 was in before OQ-064 amended it: satisfiable only by doing something other than what it says. This matters beyond tidiness. An AC whose stated method is impossible trains the reader to treat AC text as approximate, which is corrosive in a package whose whole value is that requirement text is implemented as specified. It also leaves the next reader to rediscover DEF-027 from scratch, since nothing in the AC hints that its own method is a dead end. Options: (a) amend the AC to name the SSM port-forward, which is the method actually used, needs no code change and preserves the deny; (b) leave the text and let every future verdict carry an explanatory footnote; (c) change the product so the stated method works, i.e. relax the deny.
resolution: Option (a). AC-076's statement is amended to name the SSM port-forward as the method, with the browser still driving the PUBLIC host and only the admin API tunnelled. WHAT DELIBERATELY DID NOT CHANGE is the substance being graded: the AC still requires the same three things to pass -- auth via a real Keycloak PKCE round-trip, the core governance loop, and the RTL/a11y specs -- against the real UAT environment. Only the transport for global-setup's fixture seeding is corrected, from an endpoint that returns 404 by design to one that works. THIS IS NOT LOWERING A BAR TO MAKE A VERDICT GREEN, and the ordering is the proof: the amended method is strictly harder to arrange than the original text implies, and it was executed and evidenced in AV-108 BEFORE this amendment was written, not after. Option (b) was rejected because a footnote on every future verdict is precisely the drift AGENTS.md forbids -- when code and the package disagree, fix the code or record a scope change, never let them drift silently. Option (c) was rejected for the reason DEF-027 already records: relaxing the /kc/ deny is a direct security regression that AC-081 rests on, and the SPA needs nothing under /kc/admin or /kc/realms/master, so the deny costs the product nothing. PRECEDENT: identical in shape to OQ-064, which amended AC-085 after `create-budget-action --generate-cli-skeleton` showed that the tag-scoped EC2 stop the AC described does not exist in the API at all. Both are cases where an AC was written against an assumed capability and reality disagreed; both are fixed by correcting the AC rather than by pretending. METHOD NOTE WORTH KEEPING: both impossibilities were found by ATTEMPTING the stated method against the real system and reading what came back -- response codes here, an API skeleton there. Neither would have been caught by re-reading the text, however carefully.

title: CPUCreditBalance < 50 is the wrong signal for a box that is STOPPED when idle — it makes AC-084 impose a two-hour warm-up before every e2e run, forever
question: acmp-uat-cpu-credits-low alarms when CPUCreditBalance stays under 50 for two 5-minute periods, and AC-084 requires that alarm to be untripped when an e2e run drives the box. Both are sound for a continuously-running instance. THE UAT BOX IS NOT ONE: it is deliberately stopped when idle for cost reasons (~$7.65/mo stopped vs ~$38/mo running, and the $60/mo budget is binding), and a STOPPED t3 EARNS NO CREDITS -- measured, and it corrects a claim in the previous handoff that the balance 'recovered while the box sat idle'. It had not; the alarm merely read OK because a stopped instance publishes no datapoints at all, and it returned to ALARM at ~9 credits within minutes of the box starting. A t3.medium in standard mode earns 24 credits/hour ONLY while running, and the observed net accrual on this box is roughly 15-18/hour once its own idle load is subtracted. CONSEQUENCE: from a cold start the box needs approximately TWO HOURS of running time before the alarm can clear, so as written AC-084 silently requires a two-hour warm-up before every e2e run, on every future occasion. That is a real recurring operational cost attached to an acceptance criterion, and nothing in the AC or the alarm says so. THE DEEPER QUESTION IS WHAT THE ALARM IS FOR. A low credit balance is a PERFORMANCE signal -- no burst headroom, throttled to the 20% baseline. On a long-lived server that is worth alerting on. On a box that is started on demand, spends its first two hours below the threshold by arithmetic, and is then stopped again, the alarm is in its expected state most of the time it exists, which is the definition of an alert that will be ignored. Options: (a) leave both as they are and accept the warm-up as a documented precondition of the AC; (b) keep the alarm but change what it measures, e.g. alarm on sustained CPUSurplusCreditsCharged or on low balance ONLY after the instance has been up beyond the warm-up window; (c) drop the credit clause from AC-084 and cover the risk with a direct throttling signal; (d) unlimited mode -- REJECTED on sight, since it trades a performance alarm for uncapped surplus-credit CHARGES against a binding budget, the opposite of what ADR-0034 ratified when it chose CpuCredits=standard as a SPEND control. NOT a threshold-tuning question: lowering the threshold was already considered and rejected twice (AV-104, AV-109) because it rebuilds the un-failable check the alarm exists to prevent. This asks whether the right thing is being measured.
resolution: OPTION (a) -- KEEP THE ALARM EXACTLY AS ARMED, AND DOCUMENT THE WARM-UP AS AN EXPLICIT PRECONDITION. The measurement taken to close AC-084 answered the question this OQ was asking, and it pointed the opposite way from the premise. CPUCreditUsage across the two 5-minute periods covering a full e2e run was 0.426 and 0.498, against 2.0 credits EARNED in the same window, and the balance ROSE during the run (50.09 -> 51.59). The e2e load is therefore nearly free, and the ONLY thing that ever trips this alarm is cold-start warm-up. THAT MAKES THE ALARM CORRECT RATHER THAN NOISY: during warm-up the box genuinely has no burst headroom and would be throttled to its 20% baseline under load. It is reporting a real condition that the operating model deliberately creates. OPTION (b) REJECTED because suppressing an accurate alarm until a timer elapses HIDES that real condition, and it buys a composite alarm plus metric math to silence something bounded, self-resolving and now documented. (c) rejected for the same reason. (d) rejected as recorded above. THE ARGUMENT THAT DECIDED IT IS GOVERNANCE, NOT ENGINEERING: AC-084 was earned against this exact alarm minutes before this resolution was written. Changing the control after taking a verdict from it would retroactively weaken that evidence, whatever the technical merits -- the honest order is change the control first, then re-earn the verdict. If a future session wants (b), that is the sequence. DOCUMENTED, which is the half of option (a) that makes it real rather than an opinion: deploy/runbooks/cloud-provisioning.md section 9 now carries the AC-084 row, the ~2h warm-up with the measured accrual rate, the 0.426/0.498-vs-2.0 usage figures showing the run is not the cause, the warning that a stopped instance publishes no datapoints so an OK reading while stopped means nothing, the instruction to warm up AFTER deploying since a re-bootstrap spends credits, and an explicit 'do not lower the threshold'. NOTE FOR PROD: the warm-up is an artifact of the stop-when-idle model chosen to hold UAT inside its budget. An always-on production instance never encounters it, so the alarm needs no change there either -- which is a further argument against building suppression for it.

title: UAT's backup schedule is effectively inert — cron only runs while the instance runs, and the box is stopped when idle. And nothing would report the absence, because DEF-032 alerts on a backup that FAILS, not on one that never happens
question: AC-080 is Met and the evidence is sound: a cron-triggered backup was watched to fire at 21:30:02 on 2026-08-09, crond's own journal recorded the CMD, and both .bak objects landed in s3://acmp-uat-backups/sql/ verified from off the box. That proves the schedule CAN fire. IT DOES NOT PROVE IT DOES. cron runs only while the instance runs, and this environment's operating model deliberately STOPS the box when idle (~$7.65/mo stopped vs ~$38/mo running, against a binding $60/mo budget - ADR-0034, and the same stop-when-idle model behind OQ-067). crontab.example schedules 02:00 nightly plus Sun-Thu at 08:00/12:00/16:00/20:00. The box is up for a few hours at a time, on whatever days someone is working. The overlap between those two sets is coincidental, so in practice UAT is backed up when somebody happens to have the box running at one of those minutes and not otherwise. NFR-056's RPO <= 4h and NFR-058's off-instance copy are therefore satisfied by the MECHANISM and not by the REGIME, which is the exact distinction AV-105 forced AC-080 to confront and which AV-106 resolved for the mechanism only. THE SHARPER PROBLEM IS THAT NOTHING WOULD TELL YOU. DEF-032 (fixed today) makes backup.sh publish an alert when a backup FAILS. A backup that never RUNS produces no failure, no exit code and no alert -- the silent-control shape one level up from the four already found in this project (DEF-023, DEF-030, DEF-031, DEF-032). We now detect a broken backup and remain blind to an absent one, which for a stopped box is by far the likelier state. IS THIS ACTUALLY A PROBLEM? For UAT, arguably not: it holds no data anyone would mourn, and the environment exists to be rebuilt. The risk is not the lost data, it is (i) that the package currently records AC-080 as Met in a way a reader could take as 'UAT is backed up nightly', which is untrue, and (ii) that the same stop-when-idle instinct could be carried to production, where cron would work correctly only because the box never stops -- an accident rather than a design. OPTIONS. (a) ACCEPT AND DOCUMENT: state in the runbook and on AC-080 that the schedule is inert while the box is stopped, and that NFR-056/058 depend on production being always-on. Zero cost, zero code, and it removes the misleading reading. (b) @reboot BACKUP: cronie supports @reboot, so add a line that backs up shortly after every boot. Then every session in which the box runs at all produces at least one off-instance backup, using the existing restore path unchanged. Cheap, no new infrastructure, ~20 MB to S3 per boot. Does not give a 4h RPO, but converts 'usually never' into 'at least once per session'. (c) EBS SNAPSHOTS via DLM or AWS Backup: these run REGARDLESS of instance state, and a snapshot of a STOPPED instance is genuinely consistent rather than merely crash-consistent, since nothing is writing. Attractive for exactly this operating model. But it is a volume-level recovery model, not a database restore -- it changes ADR-0033's shape, the restore runbook and the 3->0->3 drill that AC-080 is written against, and it would need its own restorability evidence. (d) EXTERNAL SCHEDULER that starts the box, backs up and stops it: real orchestration, real spend, and it partly defeats the reason the box is stopped. Recorded for completeness, not recommended. (e) DETECT THE ABSENCE, which is orthogonal to (a)-(d) and arguably the highest value of any of them: alarm on the AGE of the newest object in s3://acmp-uat-backups/sql/ rather than on the outcome of a run. That is the only option that answers 'how would we know backups had stopped?', and it composes with whichever of (a)-(d) is chosen. Note the topic-reuse caveat from AV-117 before wiring it to acmp-budget-alerts. RECOMMENDATION FOR THE OPERATOR, not a decision: (a) is the minimum honest response and costs nothing; (b)+(e) together are cheap and would make the claim in the package true rather than merely defensible. (c) deserves consideration for production but is a design change, not a fix.
